# Netplane

> Transport-independent Rust library for dynamically reconfigurable Tower service compositions.
> Generated by scripts/generate-llms-txt.sh. Version: 0.0.0

## Implemented

- Bounded Tower service execution with readiness and dispatch on the same service instance.
- Atomic publication of complete, immutable versions using ArcSwapOption.
- Synchronous version selection at Handle::execute() invocation; accepted requests retain that version until completion or future drop.
- Global synchronous admission limit across handles and versions, including unpolled futures.
- Queued-request cancellation, worker cleanup, and graceful, retryable shutdown draining.

## Limits and planned work

- Concurrency and buffer bounds are per version; the global admission budget bounds accepted, unfinished requests.
- GraphDraft validates positive capacities, not topology or application policy.
- There is no general-purpose graph construction API.
- Observability, a reconfiguration control API, HTTP integration, and general graph composition are planned.

## Workspace and authoritative documents

- [crates/netplane](crates/netplane/): Public runtime library; transport and deployment independent.
- [crates/xtask](crates/xtask/): Development tooling; never a runtime dependency.
- [README.md](README.md): Project overview and local commands.
- [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md): Coding contract and runtime invariants.
- [docs/architecture.md](docs/architecture.md): Architecture and current limits.
- [docs/architecture/execution-semantics.md](docs/architecture/execution-semantics.md): Canonical runtime behavior contract.
- [docs/adr/](docs/adr/): Accepted architectural decisions.

## Verification

Run cargo fmt --all -- --check, cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings, cargo build --workspace --all-targets, cargo test --workspace, and the live_reconfiguration example.

# Netplane

Netplane is an early stage Rust library for constructing and managing dynamically reconfigurable Tower service graphs. It aims to make graph publication, request lifetime, readiness, backpressure, and cancellation behavior explicit.

The repository provides bounded Tower service endpoints, atomic publication of validated execution versions, graceful shutdown, and development tooling. Accepted requests retain the version selected at invocation. Successful shutdown releases the active graph, even when handles remain. Version `0.0.0` marks this pre-release stage; the crate is not published.

## Scope

Netplane builds on `tower::Service`. The core is intended to be transport independent and testable with in-memory services. HTTP adapters and deployment integrations can be added later, behind real dependency boundaries. Netplane is not a standalone HTTP proxy or a replacement async runtime.

The design contract is in [docs/architecture.md](docs/architecture.md), with decisions recorded in [docs/adr](docs/adr). They distinguish current behavior from future requirements.

## Get started

The repository pins Rust 1.88 in `rust-toolchain.toml`. See [QUICKSTART.md](QUICKSTART.md) for setup and verification commands.

```bash
cargo build --workspace
cargo test --workspace
cargo run -p netplane --example live_reconfiguration
```

The workspace contains `crates/netplane` (the public library) and `crates/xtask` (development tooling). Dependencies are added only when used. `Cargo.lock` is ignored for this library workspace.

## Contribute

Read [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) and [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) before changing the architecture or public API. Report vulnerabilities through [the security policy](SECURITY.md). Netplane is licensed under [MIT](LICENSE).

# Netplane agent coding contract

Netplane is a reusable Rust library with bounded Tower execution, immutable graph-version publication, request-version retention, and graceful shutdown. Read [docs/architecture.md](docs/architecture.md), the [execution contract](docs/architecture/execution-semantics.md), and the decisions in `docs/adr/` before changing the public API.

## Workspace

| Path | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| `crates/netplane` | Public, transport-independent runtime library. |
| `crates/xtask` | Development automation; never a runtime dependency of the library. |
| `docs/architecture.md`, `docs/adr/` | Design requirements and accepted decisions. |

Add crates only when a concrete dependency boundary emerges. Keep transport and deployment adapters outside the core. Add dependencies when they have consumers, use workspace versions, and minimize dependencies exposed by the public API.

## Netplane runtime invariants

- Preserve Tower readiness and dispatch on the same service instance and selected version, including across publication.
- Publish complete immutable versions atomically. Accepted requests retain their selected version and worker resources until completion or future drop.
- Preserve queued-request cancellation, worker cleanup, immediate shutdown admission closure, and retryable draining after a timeout. Dispatched cancellation depends on the service.
- Keep `crates/netplane` independent of transports and deployment systems.
- Preserve per-version concurrency and buffer bounds. A positive global admission budget bounds accepted, unfinished requests across versions and handles, including unpolled futures.
- `GraphDraft` validates positive capacities; it does not validate topology or application policy. A general graph construction API is not implemented.

## Design rules

- Interoperate with `tower::Service` and preserve readiness semantics. Avoid a competing service abstraction without a demonstrated need.
- Keep readiness and dispatch for each request on the same service instance and graph version, including across publication.
- Validate a replacement version before publishing it. Treat published versions as immutable.
- Make ownership and request lifetime explicit so in-flight requests keep required resources through completion or cancellation.
- Bound concurrency, queues, and task creation. Never hide overload with unbounded spawning.
- Keep locks out of `.await` spans. Use `tokio` only when runtime work needs it; offload blocking or long CPU work appropriately.
- Make cancellation, timeout, and shutdown cleanup observable and testable.
- Test core behavior with mock services, without sockets. Cover version lifetime, readiness, backpressure, concurrency, cancellation, and shutdown when changing those behaviors.
- Keep future HTTP and deployment adapters outside the core runtime.

## Rust and API conventions

- Rust 2024, MSRV 1.88. Do not raise the MSRV without a dependency or feature requirement.
- Forbid unsafe code in the library. Use typed errors when needed; avoid `unwrap` and `expect` in production library code.
- Document every public item, including error and cancellation behavior. Prefer a small stable surface; keep implementation details private.
- Add or update meaningful tests before changing behavior. Inspect snapshot diffs before accepting them.
- Follow workspace lint settings. A justified lint exception belongs in the crate manifest with its reason.
- Keep source files under 500 lines. Do not put secrets or personal contact data in source or docs.
- `VERSION` and workspace version remain `0.0.0` until a deliberate release decision. The library is not currently published.

## Workflow

1. Check `git status`, nearby code, the architecture documents, and the current `.github/workflows/ci.yml` before editing.
2. Identify affected behavior and tests. Add tests first when changing logic.
3. Run focused checks. Use `./scripts/quality-gates.sh` when its optional tools are installed and its repository scan can run in the local environment. At minimum, run format, Clippy, build, and tests for code changes.
4. Update documentation when architecture or public behavior changes. Run `bash scripts/generate-llms-txt.sh` after significant architecture changes.
5. Use lowercase Conventional Commit subjects if asked to commit.

Use `rg` for repository searches and exclude `.git` and `target`. Repository skills in `.agents/skills/` contain detailed procedures, but this file is the project contract.

# Contributing to Netplane

Netplane is an early stage Rust library with bounded Tower execution, atomic version publication, cancellation, and graceful shutdown. A general graph construction API is not established. Before proposing one, read [the architecture](docs/architecture.md), [execution semantics](docs/architecture/execution-semantics.md), and [ADRs](docs/adr/), and explain how the change preserves Tower readiness, bounded resources, request lifetime, and transport independence.

## Set up

Follow [QUICKSTART.md](QUICKSTART.md) for the pinned toolchain and local commands. The workspace contains `crates/netplane` and development tooling in `crates/xtask`.

```bash
cargo fmt --all -- --check
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings
cargo build --workspace
cargo test --workspace
```

Run `./scripts/quality-gates.sh` before submitting when the required local tools are installed. Runtime changes need focused tests with in-memory Tower services.

## Changes and review

Open an [issue](https://github.com/janagor/netplane/issues) for a substantial API or architecture change, or submit a draft pull request with a small prototype. Keep changes focused and document ownership, cancellation, readiness, and error behavior for new public APIs. Changes to execution, lifecycle, or publication need appropriate tests for version selection and lifetime, concurrent publication, cancellation and resource cleanup, shutdown and worker teardown, Tower readiness, and bounded execution. Update the canonical [execution semantics](docs/architecture/execution-semantics.md) whenever runtime behavior changes. Keep transport adapters separate from the core.

Use lowercase [Conventional Commit](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/) subjects, such as `docs: establish netplane architecture`. Update documentation for changed behavior and record durable design decisions in `docs/adr/`. Pull requests should include the verification commands run and any relevant limitations.

Netplane remains at version `0.0.0` and `crates/netplane` has `publish = false`. Publishing and compatibility policy will be decided before the first usable release. Do not trigger a release as part of an ordinary contribution.

Report vulnerabilities privately through [the security policy](SECURITY.md), not a public issue.

## Source: docs/architecture.md

> Relative links in this section resolve from docs.

# Netplane architecture

## Status and purpose

Netplane is a Rust library for dynamically reconfigurable Tower service compositions. The workspace has a bounded Tower endpoint, immutable version publication, shutdown admission control, and `xtask`. [Execution semantics](architecture/execution-semantics.md) is the canonical contract for implemented runtime behavior.

## Design constraints

1. **Tower interoperability.** Compose with `tower::Service` and preserve its readiness contract. Introduce a Netplane-specific abstraction only when a working prototype shows why it is needed.
2. **Graph composition.** Model services and policies as validated executable compositions. Decide the graph representation through a small in-memory prototype.
3. **Immutable publication.** Build and validate a replacement configuration before publishing it. Active graph versions must not be modified in place.
4. **Request lifetime.** An in-flight request must retain the graph version and resources it needs until completion or cancellation. Readiness and dispatch for an individual request must operate on a consistent service instance and graph version. Graph replacement must not invalidate an outstanding readiness decision or prematurely release resources required by pending requests.
5. **Backpressure.** Bound concurrency and queues. Do not bypass readiness or spawn unbounded tasks to hide load.
6. **Cancellation and shutdown.** Define ownership and cleanup so cancellation, timeouts, and shutdown release resources without disrupting unrelated requests.
7. **Transport independence.** Core graph execution must be testable without sockets and must not depend on Hyper, Kubernetes, or a specific deployment system.
8. **Observability.** Instrument lifecycle and failures with `tracing` when the corresponding runtime behavior exists, without leaking sensitive request data.

## Workspace boundaries

| Path | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| `crates/netplane` | Public, transport-independent runtime library. Keep its public dependency surface small. |
| `crates/xtask` | Build and quality automation. Never a runtime dependency of `netplane`. |
| `docs/adr` | Accepted architectural decisions and their consequences. |

Create another crate only when a concrete dependency or API boundary justifies it. A future transport adapter may depend on the core; the core must not depend on that adapter.

## Implemented runtime

The in-memory runtime accepts a Tower service root, bounds its concurrency and buffer per version, enforces a global accepted-request budget, and publishes validated immutable versions atomically. Requests retain the version selected when `Handle::execute()` is called. Cancellation, worker ownership, and graceful shutdown follow the [execution contract](architecture/execution-semantics.md). Integration tests exercise publication, readiness, resource lifetime, and shutdown without sockets.

## Current limits and future work

A positive runtime admission limit bounds accepted, unfinished requests across all versions and handles; excess requests are rejected immediately. Validation checks positive capacities, not graph topology or application policy. There is no general-purpose graph construction API. Observability, a reconfiguration control API, HTTP integration, and broader graph composition are planned work; none are current guarantees. Arbitrary directed graphs, cycles, shared nodes, and dynamic node editing require a concrete use case before implementation.

## Decisions

- [ADR 0001: Tower service model](adr/0001-tower-service-model.md)
- [ADR 0002: Runtime reconfiguration](adr/0002-runtime-reconfiguration.md)
- [ADR 0003: Crate boundaries](adr/0003-crate-boundaries.md)

Inherited tooling ADRs in `docs/adr/tooling/` are not Netplane runtime design decisions.

## Source: docs/architecture/execution-semantics.md

> Relative links in this section resolve from docs/architecture.

# Execution semantics

This is the canonical contract for the implemented runtime. `crates/netplane` executes a Tower service root, not an arbitrary graph schema.

## Validation and publication

`GraphDraft` accepts a Tower service root, including one built with `ServiceBuilder` and layers. Validation checks positive concurrency and buffer capacities and starts a Tower buffer worker. It does not parse a graph schema, validate topology, inspect routes, or prove that an application policy is correct. The [live reconfiguration example](../../crates/netplane/examples/live_reconfiguration.rs) implements a simulated authorization filter and routing policy as ordinary Tower services.

`Handle::execute()` admits a request and selects an immutable version synchronously when called, before its returned future is polled. `Netplane::publish()` atomically replaces a complete version using `ArcSwapOption`. An accepted request keeps its selected version through completion or future drop, so an old request can finish after a new composition is published. The Tower buffer worker polls readiness and calls the same owned service instance. Requests selected after publication use the new version.

## Capacity and cancellation

Each version has its own concurrency limit and bounded Tower buffer. Capacity is not shared across retained versions; a transition can therefore have work executing in both versions. The buffer bounds queued requests, while callers waiting for queue capacity remain pending. `RuntimeLimits::max_outstanding` bounds all accepted, unfinished request futures across versions and cloned handles, including unpolled futures and queue waiters. Admission happens synchronously at `Handle::execute()` or `try_execute()` invocation. At the limit, `try_execute()` returns `AdmissionError::AtCapacity` immediately; `execute()` returns a future containing that boxed error. Completion or future drop releases one slot. Publication does not reset the budget, and old-version requests keep their slots until completion or drop. Shutdown closure takes precedence over overload. This limit does not bound tasks spawned by services or request memory. The example's router chooses between two always-ready in-memory backends, and its filter checks a caller-provided Boolean before routing. This is only a simulated authorization decision, not identity authentication.

Dropping a queued request cancels its wait. Dropping a dispatched request future releases its global admission slot, but cancellation of the underlying call depends on the service. Thus `max_outstanding` bounds accepted Netplane request futures, not all service executions that may continue after cancellation. Netplane owns each Tower buffer worker and aborts it when the last owning endpoint and request future reference disappears, including when the worker is stuck in readiness.

## Shutdown

Calling `Netplane::shutdown(grace_period)` closes admission synchronously across handles, even before its returned future is polled. Publication is rejected from that point. Shutdown waits for accepted request futures to complete or be dropped, including futures never polled. A timeout reports the outstanding count and leaves admission closed and draining, so shutdown can be retried. A successful drain clears the active graph even if inactive handles remain. Shutdown cannot forcibly reclaim resources held by an uncooperative user-owned future or tasks spawned independently inside a service.

## Outside the current runtime

General graph construction, topology and policy validation, observability, a reconfiguration control API, and HTTP integration remain future work.

## Source: docs/adr/0001-tower-service-model.md

> Relative links in this section resolve from docs/adr.

# ADR 0001: Tower service model

**Status:** Accepted

**Date:** 2026-10-14

## Context

Netplane needs a service composition model with readiness and request execution semantics. Tower already provides `Service` and `Layer`, and users should be able to integrate existing Tower components.

## Decision

Use `tower::Service` as the fundamental request-processing abstraction. Future graph composition must respect readiness before dispatching requests. Prototype any additional graph-specific API against ordinary Tower services before making it public.

## Consequences

Core tests can use in-memory mock services. An adapter may be needed for graph publication and version ownership, but it must preserve Tower interoperability. This decision does not choose a graph representation, public trait set, or runtime implementation.

## Source: docs/adr/0002-runtime-reconfiguration.md

> Relative links in this section resolve from docs/adr.

# ADR 0002: Runtime reconfiguration

**Status:** Accepted

**Date:** 2026-10-14

## Context

Changing a running service composition must not make in-flight requests observe a partially updated graph or lose resources they still need.

## Decision

Build and validate a complete replacement graph before publication. Publish graph versions immutably. A request retains the version and resources it needs until completion or cancellation; new requests may use a newer version after publication. Define shutdown behavior alongside the first implementation. Readiness and `call()` for a request must use the same service instance and graph version, even when publication occurs between those operations. Publication must preserve resources needed by an outstanding readiness decision.

## Consequences

Tests must exercise publication during active requests and between readiness and dispatch, version isolation, and cleanup after cancellation. The publication mechanism, atomicity details, reclamation strategy, and version identifier type remain open until an in-memory prototype establishes their requirements.

The first prototype uses `ArcSwapOption` for publication. Shutdown closes admission before draining accepted futures, rejects later publication, and clears the active snapshot after draining succeeds. A timed-out drain remains retryable.

Each endpoint retains the handle for its Tower buffer worker. The worker is aborted after its last endpoint and request future owner drops, so pending readiness cannot keep an obsolete version's service alive indefinitely.

## Source: docs/adr/0003-crate-boundaries.md

> Relative links in this section resolve from docs/adr.

# ADR 0003: Crate boundaries

**Status:** Accepted

**Date:** 2026-10-14

## Context

Transport dependencies can constrain reuse and make graph behavior harder to test. The workspace currently contains one library crate and `xtask`.

## Decision

Keep graph composition and execution in `crates/netplane`, independent of concrete transports and deployment systems. `xtask` remains development-only. Add another crate only when a real dependency or public API boundary is demonstrated. A future transport adapter may depend on the core; the core must not depend on the adapter.

## Consequences

Core behavior should be testable with mock Tower services and no sockets. Hyper, Kubernetes, and deployment integrations are deferred. The decision does not prohibit optional features or later crates when a prototype justifies them.

# Quick start

Netplane is a Rust library workspace. Its library crate provides bounded Tower service endpoints, atomic publication of immutable execution versions, and bounded graceful draining.

## Prerequisites

- Rust via [rustup](https://rustup.rs/); `rust-toolchain.toml` selects 1.88 with rustfmt and Clippy.
- Git for cloning the repository.
- Optional: `cargo-nextest` and the tools used by the full quality gate script.

## Build and verify

```bash
git clone https://github.com/janagor/netplane.git
cd netplane
cargo metadata --no-deps
cargo fmt --all -- --check
cargo build --workspace
cargo test --workspace
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings
```

`cargo test --workspace` includes documentation tests. If `cargo-nextest` is installed, use `cargo nextest run --workspace` for the test suite. Run `./scripts/quality-gates.sh` for the repository's broader local checks; it may require additional tools reported by the script.

Nix users can enter `nix develop`, then run the same Cargo commands. Toolchain consistency between the Nix shell and `rust-toolchain.toml` is part of the separate environment and CI work.

## Where to work

- `crates/netplane`: public library code with bounded execution, version publication, and shutdown admission.
- `crates/xtask`: repository automation, not a runtime dependency.
- `docs/architecture.md` and `docs/adr/`: design contract and decisions.
- `AGENTS.md`: coding and review instructions.

Read [the architecture](docs/architecture.md) before changing graph types or adding transport adapters. Add a dependency only with its first consumer. Keep the core independent of sockets, Hyper, Kubernetes, and specific deployment environments.

`GraphDraft::validate()` checks capacity settings and prepares an endpoint with a Tower buffer worker, so call it inside a Tokio runtime. `Netplane::publish()` swaps the active version atomically while running; requests already selected keep their previous version. `Netplane::shutdown(grace_period)` closes admission when called and returns a future that waits for accepted request futures to finish or be dropped. Successful draining releases the active graph, including when handles remain. A timeout leaves admission closed and can be retried; publication remains closed during and after shutdown.

Run the in-memory transition example with `cargo run -p netplane --example live_reconfiguration`. It changes a direct Backend A service into a router with a simulated authorization filter for Backends A and B while an old request is in progress, then drains accepted work during shutdown. See [execution semantics](docs/architecture/execution-semantics.md) for the guarantees and limits.

# Security Policy

## Supported Versions

Netplane is currently an unpublished Rust library. Security fixes are applied to
the `main` branch.

| Version | Supported |
| ------- | --------- |
| latest `main` | ✅ |
| older snapshots | ❌ |

## Reporting a Vulnerability

**Do not open a public GitHub issue for security vulnerabilities.**

Report vulnerabilities by opening a
[GitHub Security Advisory](https://github.com/janagor/netplane/security/advisories/new).

Please include:

- A description of the vulnerability
- Steps to reproduce
- Potential impact
- Suggested fix (if any)

The maintainer will respond through the private advisory channel.

## Rust-Specific Security Practices

Netplane uses the following security practices:

### Dependency Auditing

```bash
# Check advisories, licenses, banned crates, and sources
cargo deny check
```

This check runs on pull requests and pushes to `main`.

### Supply Chain Security

- `deny.toml` configures `cargo-deny` with:
  - Allowed licenses list
  - Banned crates list
  - Advisory database checks
- Dependabot is configured to propose dependency updates weekly

### Unsafe Code

- The library forbids unsafe code.

### Secrets and Credentials

- Never commit secrets, tokens, API keys, or credentials
- Use environment variables or secret management systems
- The `privacy-first` skill in `.agents/skills/privacy-first/` enforces no email
  addresses in the codebase

Repository security settings, including Dependabot alerts and branch protection,
are managed on GitHub and are separate from the checks defined in this repository.
